items.title: Google DeepMind Uses Gemini 4 Agents to Design Faster Quantum Algorithms, Verified by Lean
items.summary: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI said on Nov 23 that teams of Gemini 4 agents redesigned several quantum algorithms and circuits, with every result proved correct in Lean rather than tested on hardware. One arcsin state-loading subroutine improved 290-fold; a circuit for inertial-confinement-fusion calculations cut combined cost 11.8x and logical-qubit memory from 5,650 to 4,338. Simulations of a photosensitive molecule became 8x cheaper and cytochrome P450 modeling 2.5x, while one Grover implementation sped up 2.57x. Agents met every four hours to trade ideas in a shared notebook. The team open-sourced its Lean library, problem specifications and verified solutions.
items.impact: It demonstrates a reusable pattern for scientific discovery: agent search plus machine-checkable proofs, valuable when experiments are too costly to run. The work could shorten algorithm-design cycles for fusion and drug research, although the resulting circuits still exceed first-generation fault-tolerant hardware.

items.title: Sarvam Releases Open-Weight 105B 'Flash-Lite' Model With 160K Context and $0.15/M-Token Pricing
items.summary: Bengaluru-based Sarvam AI published Sarvam-105B-1711 on Nov 22, a new open-weight checkpoint of its 105-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model aimed at high-volume customer support, voice agents and on-premise deployment. Continued pretraining on upgraded B200 hardware extended context to 160K tokens and lifted its average across eight conversational-agent benchmarks from 42.6 to 73.9, the company says, close to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite's 74.0. A 65GB NVFP4 build fits on a single 96GB RTX PRO 6000 GPU; BF16 weights are also available. Inference optimizations cut Sarvam's blended API price from $0.44 to $0.15 per million tokens. All benchmarks are vendor-run.
items.impact: Cheap, self-hostable agents with strong Indic-language support widen options for banks and public agencies that cannot send data abroad. If independent checks hold up, the pricing could pressure Western API vendors; if not, it is another vendor-reported leaderboard claim.

items.title: Samsung Confirms Vendor Breach as n0n Leaks 150,000 Smart-TV Viewing Records
items.summary: Samsung confirmed on Nov 22 that a third-party vendor handling advertising data for Samsung Ads in North America suffered a security incident, after the n0n ransomware group dumped roughly 220MB of files on its leak site. Analysis cited from Cybernews found about 150,000 2024 smart-TV viewing events with timestamps, durations, device details, cities and ZIP codes, though not what individual viewers watched. Other sets include 42,600 political-ad records, about 99,100 AI ad-model training embeddings from 2021, and internal documents exposing an employee's details and data-warehouse infrastructure. Samsung says it is still determining scope; the vendor and affected user count remain unknown.
items.impact: The leak shows how automatic content recognition data becomes a liability once shared with processors, reviving smart-TV privacy concerns and a Texas consent agreement. For enterprises, third-party adtech remains a weak link that can expose sensitive telemetry even when core systems are untouched.

items.title: South Korean Financial Sector Hit by Fresh Breach Wave as AI-Assisted Attacks Outpace Audits
items.summary: Samsung Securities disclosed on Nov 23 that an intrusion into its Voice of Customer system on Nov 21 exposed personal data of 8,241 customers across 13 categories, including account numbers, addresses and driver's licence numbers. Yebyeol General Insurance separately reported a breach affecting 66 people via outsourced claims processor LK Insurance Brokerage. From Sept 8 to Nov 5, cyber incidents at 37 financial institutions compromised 472,619 records, a tally that excludes newer cases. The Financial Services Commission ordered more than 580 institutions to audit IT access points on Nov 5, yet attacks suspected of using AI agents have continued, exposing weaknesses in a sector long shielded by strict network segregation.
items.impact: The breaches undercut the assumption that network isolation alone protects finance and are fuelling arguments for letting Korean institutions deploy AI defensively. They also highlight outsourcing and customer-feedback systems as soft entry points that regulator-led asset inventories have yet to close.

items.title: Virginia and Oregon Sue SpaceX Over Grok Deepfakes and 'Spicy Mode' Safety Claims
items.summary: Virginia and Oregon attorneys general filed separate state-court suits on Nov 23 accusing SpaceX and its AI subsidiary of failing to stop Grok from generating sexualized images of real people, including children, and of falsely marketing Grok and X as safe. The complaints cite research by the Internet Watch Foundation and the Center for Countering Digital Hate; one study estimates about three million sexualized images were posted on X between late December and early January, roughly 23,000 appearing to depict children. The states seek injunctions, civil penalties, disgorgement and legal costs, with Virginia also seeking consumer restitution. SpaceX says it acts against misuse and notifies law enforcement.
items.impact: The first state-led suits turn AI deepfake harms into consumer-protection enforcement, bypassing a stalled federal response and Section 230 defenses. A ruling could force generators to prove safeguards work by design, not merely disclaim liability after abuse occurs.
